analysis.one_liner: Tightens taxes on people who give up U.S. citizenship to dodge taxes.
analysis.headline: The House tax committee approved the bill 20-14, but the House never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill defines when giving up U.S. citizenship counts as a move done to avoid taxes: if you paid more than $100,000 a year in income tax or your net worth is $500,000 or more, tax avoidance is presumed, and you keep paying U.S. income, estate, and gift taxes for ten years after leaving. It also covers long-term green-card holders who give up residency, requires leavers to file detailed information reports, and has the government publish their names quarterly. The bill cleared the House tax committee but never got a vote by the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers generally, who would no longer see the very wealthy erase their tax bills by renouncing citizenship; the IRS and Treasury, which gain new reporting requirements, a credit mechanism to avoid double taxation disputes, and a required report on how well former citizens actually comply. Long-term residents who never intended to leave would also be protected from a loophole that let tax-motivated leavers off easy.

how_it_helps.text: Presumes tax avoidance when the leaver paid over $100,000 in average annual income tax or held net worth of $500,000 or more, shifting the burden onto the wealthy leaver to prove otherwise (with exceptions for dual citizens, people renouncing young, and long-time absent residents).

Closes escape hatches: gains from property swaps that used to avoid recognition become taxable, and income from foreign corporations the leaver controlled (more than 50 percent ownership) counts as U.S.-source income during the ten-year window.
Extends the same rules to long-term green-card holders who drop U.S. residency or claim foreign treaty residence, closing the parallel loophole for non-citizens.

Requires anyone losing citizenship to file an information statement with assets and liabilities if wealthy, imposes penalties for failing to file, and directs quarterly publication of leavers' names in the Federal Register.
Directs Treasury to report to Congress on how well citizens and residents abroad actually comply with tax law, and to recommend improvements.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals who give up U.S. citizenship and long-term immigrant residents who give up residency: they would face U.S. income, estate, and gift taxes for ten more years, gain recognition on property swaps, tax on income from foreign companies they control, filing and penalty exposure, and public listing of their names. The rules would also apply retroactively, to citizenship losses after February 6, 1995 and to long-term residents after June 13, 1995 — both before the bill was even introduced on June 9, 1995.

drawbacks.text: The $500,000 net-worth trigger catches people far short of the ultra-rich — a retiree with a paid-off house and savings would be presumed a tax dodger and would have to request an IRS ruling within one year to escape the special rules.

The rules apply retroactively to citizenship losses after February 6, 1995 and long-term-resident changes after June 13, 1995, meaning people are taxed under rules adopted months after they acted; a limited exception exists only for those who can prove they left before February 6, 1994.

Applying the same rules to long-term residents could discourage wealthy immigrants from ever coming to or staying in the United States, since leaving after eight of fifteen years triggers the ten-year tax tail.
Enforcement was unproven: the bill itself orders Treasury to study whether former citizens actually comply, an admission that existing expatriate tax rules were poorly enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a targeted fairness measure aimed at a tiny group of the very wealthy, and its benefit to ordinary taxpayers is indirect: it protects the tax base rather than cutting anyone's bill. Its real flaws are design ones — a net-worth threshold low enough to sweep in upper-middle-class savers, and retroactivity that taxes people under rules that did not exist when they acted. The exceptions process softens the first problem but puts the burden of proof on the individual. On balance the costs fall on a narrow, wealthy population and the fairness gain is real, but the bill is blunter than it needed to be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House tax committee on a 20-14 vote and sat on the House calendar for the full House to consider, but no vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Archer, chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on June 9, 1995 with Rep. Nancy Johnson as cosponsor, and it was referred to his own committee.
The committee marked it up within four days, ordering it reported amended on a 20-14 roll-call vote on June 13, 1995.
It was reported to the House on June 16, 1995 with a written committee report and placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting full House action.
No further action was ever taken; the House never debated or voted on it, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals who renounced citizenship, and long-term residents who gave up residency after mid-1995, avoided the ten-year extension of U.S. taxes, the information filings, and the public naming that the bill would have imposed on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy people who gave up citizenship

industries.industry: High-wealth individuals who renounce U.S. citizenship
industries.note: The bill's entire target: anyone leaving with over $100,000 in annual income tax or $500,000 in net worth would be presumed a tax dodger and taxed for ten more years, with their name published quarterly. Their saving — escaping U.S. tax while keeping U.S.-built wealth — is exactly the cost shifted back to other taxpayers.

Lawful permanent residents present in 8 of 15 years who give up residency or claim foreign treaty residence would be treated like citizens who renounced, closing the non-citizen route out of U.S. taxes.

industries.industry: Foreign corporations controlled by former citizens
industries.note: Income and gains from foreign corporations more than 50 percent owned by a leaver would be treated as U.S.-source and taxed during the ten-year window, reducing the value of moving assets offshore before expatriating.
